t.3.51.1: Seeing him rising up into the sky, Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, was grief-stricken and deeply agitated, caught in great fear.
t.3.51.2: Her eyes red with anger and weeping, Sītā, as she was being carried away, cried piteously and spoke these words to the fierce-eyed lord of the rākṣasas.
t.3.51.4: Surely it was by you alone, O wicked-souled one, coward wishing to carry me off, that my husband was lured away through illusion in the form of a deer; and he too who rose up to rescue me has now been struck down.
t.3.51.3: Are you not ashamed of this deed, O vile Rāvaṇa, you who, knowing me to be alone, steal me away and flee?
t.3.51.5: Supreme indeed is the valor seen in you, O vilest of rākṣasas! For you did not proclaim your name and win me in battle.
t.3.51.6: Having done such a despicable deed, O base one, how are you not ashamed: the carrying off of a woman, and another man's woman at that, in a lonely place?
t.3.51.7: Men throughout the worlds will tell of this contemptible deed of yours, utterly cruel and most unrighteous, you who fancy yourself a hero.
t.3.51.8: Shame on your valour and your strength, of which you boasted then! Shame on such conduct of yours, which brings reproach upon your family in the world!
t.3.51.9: What can be achieved this way, that you flee by sheer speed alone? Stay even for a moment, and you will not return alive.
t.3.51.10: For once you come within the range of sight of those two princes, the sons of a king, you will not be able to live even for a moment, even with your army.
t.3.51.11: You will in no way be able to endure the touch of those two's arrows, just as a bird cannot bear the touch of a fire blazing in the forest.
t.3.51.12: Do what is right and beneficial for yourself, Rāvaṇa, and release me properly; for if you do not release me, my husband, enraged at my violation, will together with his brother bring about your destruction.
t.3.51.13: The resolve with which you wish to carry me off by force, that resolve of yours, O base one, will come to nothing.
t.3.51.14: For, not seeing that husband of mine who is like a god, and fallen into the power of my enemy, I cannot bear to keep my life for long.
t.3.51.15: Surely you do not consider what is good or wholesome for yourself; just as a mortal at the time of death resorts to things contrary to his welfare.
t.3.51.16: For to all who are about to die, what is wholesome is not pleasing. Indeed, I seem to see you bound at the throat by the noose of Death.
t.3.51.17: Since you feel no fear even in this place of danger, O Daśānana, clearly you are seeing golden trees.
t.3.51.18: O Rāvaṇa, you are beholding the dreadful river Vaitaraṇī, which carries torrents of blood, and the fearsome forest whose leaves are swords.
t.3.51.19: You will see the sharp śālmalī tree, with flowers of molten gold and leaves of the finest vaiḍūrya gems, covered all over with thorns of iron.
t.3.51.20: Having done such a wrong to that great-souled one, you will surely not be able to survive for long, like a heartless man who has drunk poison.
t.3.51.21: You are bound, Rāvaṇa, by the noose of Time, which is hard to ward off. Where can you go and find shelter from my great-souled husband?
t.3.51.22: He by whom fourteen thousand rākṣasas were slain in battle within the mere space of the twinkling of an eye, without his brother's help.
t.3.51.23: How could that heroic Rāghava, mighty and skilled in all weapons, not slay you with his sharp arrows, you who have carried off his beloved wife?
t.3.51.24: Seated on Rāvaṇa's lap, Vaidehī, overwhelmed by fear and grief, lamented piteously, uttering these and other harsh words.
t.3.51.25: The beautiful lady had lamented piteously before; and the wicked one carried off the young princess, so sorely distressed and speaking much, as she writhed, a trembling having come over her limbs.
